claim: Sex-specific triacylglycerides are broadly conserved across the subgenus Drosophila in 11 species.
source: Here we show that sex-specific triacylclyerides (TAGs) are broadly conserved across the subgenus Drosophila in 11 species and represent a novel class of pheromones that has been largely overlooked.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by the phylogenetic analysis and UV-LDI MS data presented in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sex-specific TAGs represent a novel class of pheromones that has been largely overlooked.
source: Here we show that sex-specific triacylclyerides (TAGs) are broadly conserved across the subgenus Drosophila in 11 species and represent a novel class of pheromones that has been largely overlooked.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the novelty of the structural characterization and functional behavioral data throughout the manuscript.

claim: In desert-adapted drosophilids, 13 different TAGs are secreted exclusively by males from the ejaculatory bulb.
source: In desert-adapted drosophilids, 13 different TAGs are secreted exclusively by males from the ejaculatory bulb, transferred to females during mating, and function synergistically to inhibit courtship from other males.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by UV-LDI MS data in Figure 2 and dissection experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sex-specific TAGs are transferred to females during mating.
source: In desert-adapted drosophilids, 13 different TAGs are secreted exclusively by males from the ejaculatory bulb, transferred to females during mating, and function synergistically to inhibit courtship from other males.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by UV-LDI MS detection of TAGs on mated females in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sex-specific TAGs function synergistically to inhibit courtship from other males.
source: In desert-adapted drosophilids, 13 different TAGs are secreted exclusively by males from the ejaculatory bulb, transferred to females during mating, and function synergistically to inhibit courtship from other males.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by behavioral assays showing synergistic effects of TAG combinations in Figure 5F, G, H, and I.

claim: Sex-specific TAGs are comprised of at least one short branched tiglic acid and a long linear fatty acyl component.
source: Sex-specific TAGs are comprised of at least one short branched tiglic acid and a long linear fatty acyl component, an unusual structural motif that has not been reported before in other natural products.
evidence: This structural characterization is stated in the abstract and supported by GCMS, CID MS, and OzID MS data in Figure 3 and supplementary figures.

claim: The structural motif of sex-specific TAGs (short branched tiglic acid with long linear fatty acyl component) has not been reported before in other natural products.
source: Sex-specific TAGs are comprised of at least one short branched tiglic acid and a long linear fatty acyl component, an unusual structural motif that has not been reported before in other natural products.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and discussed in the Discussion section with reference to conventional TAGs in natural products.

claim: The diversification of chemical cues used by desert-adapted Drosophila as pheromones may be related to their specialized diet of fermenting cacti.
source: The diversification of chemical cues used by desert-adapted Drosophila as pheromones may be related to their specialized diet of fermenting cacti.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a hypothesis and discussed in the Discussion section with reference to diet effects shown in Figure 4.

claim: Chemical signatures consistent with TAG structures were found to be largely conserved across 3 different Drosophila groups: the repleta radiation, the virilis group, and the robusta group.
source: Chemical signatures consistent with TAG structures were found to be largely conserved across 3 different Drosophila groups: the repleta radiation (including Drosophila hydei, Drosophila buzzatii, Drosophila navojoa, Drosophila wheeleri, and Drosophila aldrichi), the virilis group (Drosophila americana, Drosophila virilis, and Drosophila montana), and within the robusta group (Drosophila robusta) (Figure 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by UV-LDI MS data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: TAGs were expressed only in the ejaculatory bulb of males.
source: The TAGs were expressed only in the ejaculatory bulb of males.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by dissection and UV-LDI MS analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sex-specific TAGs were not detected in any of the species tested from the Sophophora subgenus.
source: In contrast, sex-specific TAGs were not detected in any of the species tested from the Sophophora subgenus.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the phylogenetic analysis in Figure 1 showing no TAG production in Sophophora species.

claim: Many of the TAG-producing species are capable of feeding and reproducing on cacti, fungi (mushroom), and tree sap or slime fluxes.
source: Many of the TAG-producing species are capable of feeding and reproducing on cacti, fungi (mushroom), and tree sap or slime fluxes, substrates that contain high levels of toxins, plant defensive compounds, or bacteria, a characteristic that may be related to their ability to produce sex-specific TAGs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 1 with diet icons, drawing on previous literature about these species' diets.

claim: UV-LDI MS detected 13 TAGs and several long-chain acetyldienyl acetates exclusively in the anogenital region of D. arizonae and D. mojavensis males and not on virgin females.
source: Analysis by UV-LDI MS detected 13 TAGs and several long-chain acetyldienyl acetates, 30 or 32 carbons in length (referred to as long OAcs) exclusively in the anogenital region of D. arizonae and D. mojavensis males and not on virgin females of either species (Figure 2A,B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A and B with mass spectra from male anogenital regions.

claim: The expression of TAGs and long OAcs increased in abundance as D. arizonae males matured, with little or no expression in the first 4 days after eclosion.
source: Chemical profiling of D. arizonae from 0 to 15 days old indicated that the expression of the TAGs and long OAcs increased in abundance as males get matured, with little or no expression in the first 4 days after eclosion and higher expression towards the age of maturity at approximately 8 day old, the age when males exhibit full courtship behaviors (Markow, 1981) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C with age-dependent expression data.

claim: D. arizonae males exhibit full courtship behaviors at approximately 8 days old.
source: Chemical profiling of D. arizonae from 0 to 15 days old indicated that the expression of the TAGs and long OAcs increased in abundance as males get matured, with little or no expression in the first 4 days after eclosion and higher expression towards the age of maturity at approximately 8 day old, the age when males exhibit full courtship behaviors (Markow, 1981) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to Markow, 1981.

claim: D. mojavensis followed a similar maturation profile to D. arizonae for TAG and long OAc expression.
source: D. mojavensis followed a similar maturation profile (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Analysis of dissected male reproductive organs by UV-LDI MS revealed qualitatively similar chemical profiles exclusively in the ejaculatory bulbs.
source: Analysis of dissected male reproductive organs by UV-LDI MS revealed qualitatively similar chemical profiles exclusively in the ejaculatory bulbs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: No predicted precursors of TAGs such as diacylglycerol or glycerol-3-phosphate were detected from the accessory glands or other reproductive organs.
source: In addition, no predicted precursors of these compounds such as diacylglycerol or glycerol-3-phosphate were detected from the accessory glands or other reproductive organs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on UV-LDI MS analysis of dissected tissues.

claim: TAGs and long OAcs are synthesized in the ejaculatory bulb.
source: These results indicate that the TAGs and long OAcs are synthesized in the ejaculatory bulb.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section based on the exclusive detection of these compounds in the ejaculatory bulb and absence of precursors elsewhere.

claim: Chemical derivatization of the long OAc fraction confirmed the presence of an acetyl group.
source: Chemical derivatization of the long OAc fraction confirmed the presence of an acetyl group (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: GCMS analysis of transesterified TLC fractions indicated tiglic acid as one of the fatty acyl moieties.
source: Gas chromatography MS (GCMS) analysis of transesterified TLC fractions indicated tiglic acid, a 5-carbon branched unsaturated acid, as one of the fatty acyl moieties (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: No other 5-carbon fatty acid methyl esters were detected besides tiglic acid.
source: No other 5-carbon fatty acid methyl esters were detected.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on GCMS analysis.

claim: Each TAG molecule contains a single long-chain fatty acyl component (16–18 carbons in length) together with 2 short-chain fatty acyl side chains (each 2–5 carbons in length).
source: A similar motif was revealed among each of the molecules: a single long-chain fatty acyl component, 16–18 carbons in length, together with 2 short-chain fatty acyl side chains, each 2–5 carbons in length (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 4 based on CID MS analysis.

claim: For several abundant TAG molecules, long-chain fatty acids are predominantly located at either sn-1 or sn-3 position on the glycerol backbone.
source: Based on this observation, long-chain fatty acids are predominantly located at either sn-1 or sn-3 for the major TAGs at [M + Na]+ 543 and 541 (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 4) and [M + Li]+ 499, 501, and 527 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on CID MS fragmentation patterns following the method of Hsu and Turk (1999 and 2010).

claim: It was not possible to distinguish between sn-1 and sn-3 positions for the long-chain fatty acids.
source: It was not possible to distinguish between sn-1 and sn-3 positions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a limitation of the CID MS method.

claim: The position assignments on the glycerol backbone are supported by analysis of synthetic standards.
source: The position assignments on the backbone are supported by analysis of synthetic standards in which a long-chain fatty acid is placed at sn-1. The relative abundances of fragment ions are similar to those observed from crude extract (Figure 3—figure supplement 6–8).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6–8.

claim: CID analysis of TAG at [M + Li]+ 487 suggests that the C18:1 fatty acyl substituent is likely at the sn-2 position.
source: Notably, CID analysis of a fourth major TAG at [M + Li]+ 487 resulted in low-intensity signals corresponding to loss of the C18:1 fatty acyl substituent, suggesting that this component is likely to reside at the sn-2 position (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on CID MS fragmentation patterns.

claim: OzID analysis of the TAG fraction revealed numerous positional isomers with double bond positions at n-9, n-7, and n-2.
source: OzID analysis of the TAG fraction revealed numerous positional isomers, with double bond positions between C9-C10 (n-9) and C11-C12 (n-7), indicating oleic and palmitoleic acid side chains, and between C2-C3 (n-2), consistent with tiglic acid (Figure 3B,C; Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3B, C and Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: Double bond positions at n-9 and n-7 indicate oleic and palmitoleic acid side chains.
source: OzID analysis of the TAG fraction revealed numerous positional isomers, with double bond positions between C9-C10 (n-9) and C11-C12 (n-7), indicating oleic and palmitoleic acid side chains, and between C2-C3 (n-2), consistent with tiglic acid (Figure 3B,C; Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on OzID MS analysis and knowledge of fatty acid structures.

claim: Double bond position at n-2 is consistent with tiglic acid.
source: OzID analysis of the TAG fraction revealed numerous positional isomers, with double bond positions between C9-C10 (n-9) and C11-C12 (n-7), indicating oleic and palmitoleic acid side chains, and between C2-C3 (n-2), consistent with tiglic acid (Figure 3B,C; Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on OzID MS analysis and knowledge of tiglic acid structure.

claim: The relative abundance of aldehyde and Criegee ions for TAGs at [M + Na]+ 543 and 541 are consistent with cis-double bonds.
source: The relative abundance of the aldehyde and Criegee ions for the molecules at [M + Na]+ 543 and 541 are consistent with those of synthetic TAG standards synthesized with oleic acid and linoleic acid, both of which contain cis- double bonds (Figure 3—figure supplement 6 and 8).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on comparison with synthetic standards in OzID MS analysis.

claim: All of the analyzed TAGs contained tiglic acid.
source: All of the analyzed TAGs contained tiglic acid.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a summary of the structural analysis.

claim: The unusual combination of short odd-branched chain fatty acids with a single linear long-chain component has not been reported before in natural products.
source: The unusual combination of short odd-branched chain fatty acids with a single linear long-chain component has not been reported before in natural products.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on comparison with known natural product structures.

claim: Males raised on standard media produced a significantly lower amount of some sex-specific TAGs compared to males raised on cactus-banana supplemented media.
source: Thin layer chromatography of the lipid contents of ejaculatory bulbs indicated that males raised on standard media produced a significantly lower amount of some of the sex-specific TAGs, including [M + K]+ 559, one of the most abundant molecules (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4 with statistical analysis.

claim: A specialized diet is not essential for sex-specific TAG production.
source: The results show that although a specialized diet is not essential for sex-specific TAG production, precursors derived from food can influence the quantity of several of the TAGs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the observation that TAGs are still produced on standard media, though at lower levels.

claim: Precursors derived from food can influence the quantity of several TAGs.
source: The results show that although a specialized diet is not essential for sex-specific TAG production, precursors derived from food can influence the quantity of several of the TAGs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the diet experiment shown in Figure 4.

claim: Males from D. arizonae and D. mojavensis were significantly more attracted to virgin females than recently mated females.
source: Males from D. arizonae and D. mojavensis were significantly more attracted to virgin females than recently mated females (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5B with statistical analysis.

claim: Significant levels of both TAGs and long OAcs were found on the anogenital regions of D. arizonae females shortly after mating.
source: Notably, significant levels of both TAGs and long OAcs were found on the anogenital regions of D. arizonae females shortly after mating but decreased by approximately 80% at 2–4 hr post-mating and were almost negligible at 8 hr post-mating (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: TAGs and long OAcs on mated D. arizonae females decreased by approximately 80% at 2–4 hr post-mating.
source: Notably, significant levels of both TAGs and long OAcs were found on the anogenital regions of D. arizonae females shortly after mating but decreased by approximately 80% at 2–4 hr post-mating and were almost negligible at 8 hr post-mating (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: TAGs and long OAcs on mated D. arizonae females were almost negligible at 8 hr post-mating.
source: Notably, significant levels of both TAGs and long OAcs were found on the anogenital regions of D. arizonae females shortly after mating but decreased by approximately 80% at 2–4 hr post-mating and were almost negligible at 8 hr post-mating (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Mated D. arizonae females became increasingly attractive over time, correlating with a decrease of the levels of TAGs and long OAcs on the cuticle.
source: Mated D. arizonae females became increasingly attractive over time, correlating with a decrease of the levels of TAGs and long OAcs on the cuticle (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5D.

claim: From 4 hr onwards post-mating, males showed no significant preference between mated and virgin D. arizonae females.
source: From 4 hr onwards, males showed no significant preference between mated and virgin females.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on behavioral assays shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Female remating was observed starting only at 8 hr post-mating.
source: Female remating was observed starting only at 8 hr post-mating (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The presence of male-transferred lipids on female cuticles is accompanied by a concomitant decrease in female attractiveness.
source: Taken together, these results show that the presence of male-transferred lipids on female cuticles is accompanied by a concomitant decrease in female attractiveness.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section based on the correlation between TAG levels and attractiveness over time.

claim: Fewer males from D. arizonae, D. mojavensis, and D. navojoa chose to initiate courtship with extract-perfumed females compared to solvent-perfumed females.
source: In these species, fewer males chose to initiate courtship with extract-perfumed females (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5E with statistical analysis.

claim: D. arizonae was significantly less likely to copulate with bulb-perfumed females.
source: D. arizonae was also significantly less likely to copulate with bulb-perfumed females, whereas D. mojavensis showed a tendency to avoid perfumed females (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: D. mojavensis showed a tendency to avoid perfumed females in copulation choice.
source: D. arizonae was also significantly less likely to copulate with bulb-perfumed females, whereas D. mojavensis showed a tendency to avoid perfumed females (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The use of sex-specific TAGs as anti-aphrodisiacs is conserved across several species.
source: These results suggest that the use of these sex-specific TAGs as anti-aphrodisiacs is conserved across several species.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section based on behavioral data from multiple species.

claim: The higher the concentration of ejaculatory bulb extract, the greater the aversion exhibited by D. arizonae males.
source: Further analysis of D. arizonae indicated that the higher the concentration of the extract, the greater the aversion exhibited by males.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on dose-response experiments shown in Figure 5E.

claim: A minimum dose of extract from approximately 0.5 ejaculatory bulbs was needed to achieve a significant behavioral effect in D. arizonae.
source: A minimum dose of extract from approximately 0.5 ejaculatory bulbs was needed to achieve a significant behavioral effect (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Ejaculatory bulb extract from immature males did not suppress male courtship.
source: Ejaculatory bulb extract from immature males (and therefore, containing negligible amounts of TAGs and long OAcs) did not suppress male courtship (Figure 5E; Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Courtship inhibition is not a generalized aversion to other compounds extracted from ejaculatory bulb tissue.
source: Thus, courtship inhibition is not a generalized aversion to other compounds extracted from ejaculatory bulb tissue.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section based on the lack of effect from immature bulb extracts.

claim: Female rejection behavior was not a major contributing factor to copulation choice in perfuming experiments.
source: Since virgin females were used, female rejection behavior was not a major contributing factor to copulation choice.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the experimental design using virgin females.

claim: It is unlikely that female rejection behavior was triggered by females' sensory feedback from perfuming.
source: Furthermore, it is unlikely that female rejection behavior was triggered by females' sensory feedback from perfuming. D. arizonae males continued to avoid mating with perfumed females from which the major olfactory and gustatory organs have been removed (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: The presence of male-specific long OAcs and TAGs on females was sufficient to fully recapitulate the loss of attractiveness observed in recently mated females.
source: Taken together, the presence of male-specific long OAcs and TAGs on females was sufficient to fully recapitulate the loss of attractiveness observed in recently mated females.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section based on perfuming experiments.

claim: Perfuming with both long OAcs and TAGs strongly suppressed courtship initiation and copulation.
source: Perfuming with both long OAcs and TAGs strongly suppressed courtship initiation and copulation (Figure 5F,G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5F and G.

claim: The presence of TAGs alone significantly reduced the likelihood of copulation.
source: The presence of TAGs alone significantly reduced the likelihood of copulation (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Long OAcs had an attractive effect when used alone.
source: Interestingly, long OAcs had an attractive effect when used alone (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Both TAGs and long OAcs are needed to suppress courtship initiation.
source: These results suggest that both TAGs and long OAcs are needed to suppress courtship initiation, whereas TAGs are important for discouraging later stages of courtship.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section based on the differential effects of TAGs and long OAcs alone versus combined.

claim: TAGs are important for discouraging later stages of courtship.
source: These results suggest that both TAGs and long OAcs are needed to suppress courtship initiation, whereas TAGs are important for discouraging later stages of courtship.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section based on the effect of TAGs alone on copulation.

claim: TAGs containing oleic acid or linoleic acid significantly suppressed courtship initiation when combined with long OAcs.
source: Males were given a choice of solvent-perfumed females or females perfumed with a single TAG species together with long OAcs. Under these conditions, TAGs containing oleic acid or linoleic acid significantly suppressed courtship initiation (Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: Only the TAG containing oleic acid was capable of suppressing copulation at a dose of 75 ng per female.
source: However, only the former was capable of suppressing copulation as well and at a dose of 75 ng per female (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Only the (R) configuration of the oleic acid-containing TAG was bioactive.
source: Moreover, only the (R) configuration of this TAG was bioactive (Figure 5H; Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: Perfuming females with the (S)-enantiomer of the oleic acid-containing TAG showed no significant effect on male choice.
source: Perfuming females with the (S)-enantiomer showed no significant effect on male choice, signifying that courtship aversion is specific to the stereochemistry of the TAG and not due to general avoidance of a foreign molecule or masking of female aphrodisiacs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on behavioral assays with the (S)-enantiomer.

claim: Courtship aversion is specific to the stereochemistry of the TAG and not due to general avoidance of a foreign molecule or masking of female aphrodisiacs.
source: Perfuming females with the (S)-enantiomer showed no significant effect on male choice, signifying that courtship aversion is specific to the stereochemistry of the TAG and not due to general avoidance of a foreign molecule or masking of female aphrodisiacs.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section based on the stereospecific effect.

claim: Two combinations of TAGs reduced copulation: 1-steroyl-2,3-ditigloyl glycerol with 1-oleoyl-2,3-ditigloyl glycerol, and 1-steroyl-2,3-ditigloyl glycerol with 1-linoleyl-2,3-ditiglyoyl glycerol.
source: However, two combinations of TAGs reduced copulation: 1-steroyl-2,3-ditigloyl glycerol together with either 1-oleoyl-2,3-ditigloyl glycerol or 1-linoleyl-2,3-ditiglyoyl glycerol (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Both TAG combinations that reduced copulation also inhibited courtship initiation.
source: Both combinations also inhibited courtship initiation (Figure 5—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 6.

claim: Low amounts of several TAG species, inactive on their own, can act in synergy with each other to suppress male courtship and copulation.
source: Thus, low amounts of several TAG species, inactive on their own, can act in synergy with each other to suppress male courtship and copulation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section based on the synergistic effects observed with TAG combinations.

claim: None of the TAG combinations tested were effective without long OAcs.
source: It is notable that none of the TAG combinations tested were effective without long OAcs despite our finding that a mixture of TAGs purified from extract was by itself sufficient to deter male attraction.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the synthetic TAG experiments.

claim: A combination of several different TAG species may be needed for courtship inhibition without the presence of long OAcs.
source: It may be the case that a combination of several different TAG species is needed for courtship inhibition without the presence of long OAcs.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the Results section to explain the discrepancy between natural extract and synthetic TAG combinations.

claim: TAGs are a novel class of mating-related pheromones used by males to manipulate the post-mating attractiveness of females.
source: Our results show that TAGs are a novel class of mating-related pheromones that are used by males to manipulate the post-mating attractiveness of females.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion section based on the behavioral and chemical data.

claim: Earlier studies of D. arizonae and D. mojavensis cuticular lipids using GCMS found mostly linear and branched long-chain hydrocarbons.
source: Earlier studies of D. arizonae and D. mojavensis cuticular lipids using GCMS found mostly linear and branched long-chain hydrocarbons, including dienes, trienes, and methyl-branched alkenes, 29–38 carbons in length (Toolson et al., 1990; Etges and Jackson, 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to previous studies.

claim: TAGs were not previously observed in D. arizonae and D. mojavensis likely due to analytical limitations.
source: TAGs were not previously observed likely due to analytical limitations; under standard GCMS conditions, heavier molecules such as TAGs are not detected.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an explanation for why TAGs were overlooked in previous studies.

claim: Under standard GCMS conditions, heavier molecules such as TAGs are not detected.
source: TAGs were not previously observed likely due to analytical limitations; under standard GCMS conditions, heavier molecules such as TAGs are not detected.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a technical limitation of GCMS.

claim: Sex-specific TAGs are structurally distinct from conventional TAGs found in other Drosophila tissues.
source: Second, sex-specific TAGs are structurally distinct from conventional TAGs found in other Drosophila tissues (Carvalho et al., 2012; Guan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to studies on conventional TAGs.

claim: Short UV-LDI MS analysis times cause minimal perturbation of the cuticle.
source: Last, short UV-LDI MS analysis times (below 30 s, corresponding to 1200 laser shots) causes minimal perturbation of the cuticle; breakdown of the outer layers appear only after 2000 laser shots (Yew et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to a previous methodological study.

claim: The parasitic wasp Lariophagus distinguendus uses TAGs together with a branched alkane to promote mating behavior.
source: The parasitic wasp Lariophagus distinguendus was recently reported to use TAGs together with a branched alkane to promote mating behavior (Kühbandner et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation.

claim: Food odors are known to synergize with aggregation pheromones in beetles.
source: Food odors are also known to synergize with aggregation pheromones in beetles (Lin et al., 1992) and with sex pheromones in Drosophila (Grosjean et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations.

claim: Food odors synergize with sex pheromones in Drosophila.
source: Food odors are also known to synergize with aggregation pheromones in beetles (Lin et al., 1992) and with sex pheromones in Drosophila (Grosjean et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation.

claim: Pheromonal synergism between completely different classes of molecules is rare.
source: Pheromonal synergism between completely different classes of molecules is rare and may be a mechanism to increase combinatorial complexity.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on comparison with known examples of pheromone synergism.

claim: Pheromonal synergism between different classes of molecules may be a mechanism to increase combinatorial complexity.
source: Pheromonal synergism between completely different classes of molecules is rare and may be a mechanism to increase combinatorial complexity.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the Discussion section.

claim: Only some of the D. arizonae TAGs appear to play a role as an anti-aphrodisiac.
source: Interestingly, only some of the D. arizonae TAGs appear to play a role as an anti-aphrodisiac.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the differential bioactivity of synthetic TAGs.

claim: The quiescent stereoisomers of TAGs could be used as potential future chemical cues.
source: The quiescent stereoisomers could be used as potential future chemical cues (Niehuis et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the Discussion section with a citation.

claim: Conventional naturally occurring TAGs found in plant oils and animal fat typically consist of linear fatty acyl moieties that have 16, 18, or 20 carbons.
source: Conventional naturally occurring TAGs found in plant oils and animal fat typically consist of linear fatty acyl moieties that have 16, 18, or 20 carbons (Nelson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation.

claim: Medium and short chain fatty acyls have been found in TAGs from whale blubber and bovine milk fat, respectively.
source: Although medium and short chain fatty acyls have been found in TAGs from, respectively, whale blubber (Litchfield et al., 1971) and bovine milk fat (Breckenridge and Kuksis, 1968), they are only in combination with linear and even-numbered carbon acyls.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations.

evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to previous work and reference to Figure 4.

source: For example, desert-adapted D. arizonae and D. mojavensis feed on fermenting cacti, which have high levels of triterpene glycosides, medium chain fatty acids, and sterol diols, compounds which can serve as toxic plant defense chemicals (Fogleman and Danielson, 2001).

claim: Bacterial wetwood infections produce acetate, butyrate, valerate, hexanoate, and propionate.
source: Bacterial wetwood infections have been shown to produce acetate, butyrate, valerate, hexanoate, and propionate (Ward and Zeikus, 1980), which could be directly incorporated into the TAGs or serve as precursors for branched or linear fatty acids, as has been observed for nitidulid beetles (Carpophilus spp) (Bartelt and Weisleder, 1996).

claim: Compounds from bacterial wetwood infections could be directly incorporated into TAGs or serve as precursors for branched or linear fatty acids.
source: Bacterial wetwood infections have been shown to produce acetate, butyrate, valerate, hexanoate, and propionate (Ward and Zeikus, 1980), which could be directly incorporated into the TAGs or serve as precursors for branched or linear fatty acids, as has been observed for nitidulid beetles (Carpophilus spp) (Bartelt and Weisleder, 1996).
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the Discussion section with citations.

claim: Enzymes used for detoxification may have been adapted for TAG synthesis in drosophilids that produce sex-specific TAGs.
source: The ability of drosophilids that produce sex-specific TAGs to thrive on these specialized substrates alludes to the possibility that enzymes used for detoxification may have been adapted for TAG synthesis.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the Discussion section.

source: Notably, cytochrome P450 monooxygenases have been identified in other insects as playing a crucial role in detoxification and cuticular lipid synthesis (Li et al., 2004; Qiu et al., 2012).

claim: Conservation of TAG expression may be more related to phylogenetic effects than functional adaptation.

claim: Desert-adapted drosophilids are capable of using precursors from the environment and synthesizing the components de novo.
source: Thus, desert-adapted drosophilids are capable of using precursors from the environment and synthesizing the components de novo though significant quantitative differences are found for some TAG molecules.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the observation that TAGs are produced on both standard and supplemented diets.

claim: Both dietary sequestration and de novo production pathways are used by numerous Coleoptera beetle species for the production of aggregation pheromones.
source: Both pathways for precursor synthesis are used by numerous Coleoptera beetle species for the production of aggregation pheromones (Tillman et al., 1999).

claim: The ability to utilize different production pathways may enable insects to switch host plants while preserving conspecific signaling.

claim: Pheromones are produced by oenocytes in both males and females and the male ejaculatory bulb in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, pheromones are produced by oenocytes (specialized epithelial cells in both males and females) and the male ejaculatory bulb and subsequently secreted onto the cuticular surface and anogenital region, respectively (Billeter et al., 2009; Yew et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations.
